questions.questionMd: To allow a form to submit when the user presses the Enter key, in addition to clicking a button, what must you do in your HTML?

options.text: Add a `keydown` event listener directly to the input element and manually check whether the key pressed has the code value of `Enter` each time a keystroke occurs
Wrap the input elements inside a `<form>` element and listen for the `submit` event on that form
Set the `autocomplete` attribute on the input element to `on` so that the browser automatically triggers submission when it detects a confirmed input value
Use a `<button type="button">` element paired with a global document-level `keypress` listener that checks for the Enter key on every page interaction

questions.explanationMd: Putting the inputs inside a `<form>` lets the browser trigger the form's `submit` event when the user presses Enter, so the same submit handler can handle both Enter and button submission.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, why can multiple images load in parallel even though JavaScript is single-threaded?

options.text: Image loading is handled entirely by the operating system's DNS resolver and network stack, which feeds completed image buffers directly into the browser's graphics memory
The browser itself is multi-threaded and multi-process, so network requests and image decoding happen in browser threads outside the JavaScript runtime
The browser batches all image requests into a single multiplexed HTTP/2 stream that the JavaScript engine processes sequentially but displays simultaneously after all bytes arrive
JavaScript uses Web Workers internally for all image element operations, with each image object spawning its own dedicated worker thread to manage the download lifecycle

questions.explanationMd: JavaScript execution is single-threaded, but the browser has other threads and processes for networking, decoding, rendering, and resource loading. That is why several image downloads can progress in parallel.

questions.questionMd: In a URL query string, how are query parameter key-value pairs structured?

options.text: Each pair is formatted as `{param, value}` using curly-brace destructuring syntax borrowed from JavaScript ES6 to maintain consistency with the client-side code that builds the URL
Each pair is formatted as `param:value` using a colon separator, consistent with the JSON object notation used in the response body returned by RESTful endpoints
Each pair is formatted as `param=value`, where the parameter name and its value are separated by an equals sign
Each pair is formatted as `param/value` using a slash separator, following the hierarchical path convention used in the base URL segment of RESTful API endpoints

questions.explanationMd: Query parameters use the `key=value` format, such as `?q=music` or `?type=album`.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, what is a simple way to check whether a particular company or product offers a publicly accessible developer API?

options.text: Search for `<product name> API` using a search engine to see if a developer API exists
Send an HTTP OPTIONS request to the company's main domain and inspect the Allow header in the response to discover the supported API endpoints and methods
Check the W3C's official registry of public REST APIs, which every company is required to register with before making its API available to third-party developers
Use the browser's Network tab to inspect all requests made by the company's website, then reverse-engineer those endpoints to determine which ones accept external calls

questions.explanationMd: A practical first step is to search for the product or company name together with `API`, which often leads to official developer documentation if one exists.

questions.questionMd: Consider this code: `console.log('A'); setTimeout(fn, 3000); console.log('B');` In what order will the console outputs appear?

options.text: `B`, then `A`, then the output from `fn`, because the JavaScript engine hoists `setTimeout` calls to the top of the execution context before running any other statements
`A`, then the output from `fn` after 3 seconds, then `B`, because `setTimeout` blocks the call stack for the specified duration before allowing subsequent synchronous code to run
The output from `fn`, then `A`, then `B`, because `setTimeout` callbacks are placed in the Micro-task Queue which has higher priority than synchronous code on the call stack
`A`, then `B`, then whatever `fn` logs after approximately 3 seconds

questions.explanationMd: `console.log('A')` runs first, `setTimeout` schedules `fn` for later, and `console.log('B')` runs immediately after. The callback runs later after the timer delay.

questions.questionMd: In JavaScript, how do you read the current text entered by a user in an `<input type="text">` element?

options.text: `inputElement.textContent`
`inputElement.innerHTML`
`inputElement.value`
`inputElement.data`

questions.explanationMd: For form controls such as text inputs, the user's current typed value is stored in the element's `.value` property.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, which company introduced Falcor as a REST alternative?

options.text: Amazon, which required a uniform data-access abstraction across its many distributed AWS services that had diverse underlying data formats
Netflix
Facebook, which needed a declarative data-fetching layer for its React-based front-end after experiencing performance problems with traditional REST endpoints
Microsoft, which built it as an open-source project to simplify data binding between Azure cloud services and JavaScript single-page applications

questions.explanationMd: Falcor is associated with Netflix and was introduced as an alternative model for accessing remote data.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, in which year did Facebook open-source GraphQL?
questions.explanationMd: The lecture marks 2015 as the year Facebook open-sourced GraphQL.

questions.questionMd: What HTTP method does the `fetch()` API use by default when no options object is provided?

options.text: HEAD
POST
GET
OPTIONS

questions.explanationMd: A basic `fetch(url)` request uses the HTTP `GET` method unless another method is specified in the options object.

questions.questionMd: What is the key advantage of using arrow functions (`=>`) as callbacks in `fetch().then()` chains compared to ordinary functions?

options.text: Arrow functions convert the Promise returned by `fetch()` into a plain value synchronously, eliminating the need for chained `.then()` calls in most use cases
Arrow functions execute synchronously instead of asynchronously, which ensures that the callback completes before any subsequent line of code in the method runs
Arrow functions bypass the browser's CORS policy because they use a different internal request mechanism that does not carry an Origin header in the HTTP request
Arrow functions are automatically bound to the `this` value of their enclosing context, so they do not create their own `this` binding

questions.explanationMd: Arrow functions do not create their own `this`; they capture `this` lexically from the surrounding scope. This makes them useful inside class methods and Promise chains.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture's definition, what is a “gotcha” in programming?

options.text: A valid construct that works as documented but is counter-intuitive and almost invites mistakes because it is easy to invoke and unexpected in its outcome
A security vulnerability in a programming language runtime that attackers can exploit to execute arbitrary code by supplying malformed input to a parsing function
A deprecated API function that still exists in the language specification for backward compatibility but produces incorrect results when called in strict mode environments
A deliberate bug intentionally left in a codebase by a developer to test whether automated testing pipelines are comprehensive enough to catch subtle logic errors

questions.explanationMd: A programming gotcha is a valid language feature or behavior that is easy to use incorrectly because it produces surprising or counter-intuitive results.

questions.questionMd: In a URL query string, which character separates subsequent non-first query parameters from each other?

options.text: `;` (semicolon)
`=` (equals sign)

questions.explanationMd: After the first query parameter begins with `?`, additional query parameters are separated with `&`, for example `?q=test&page=2`.

questions.questionMd: When constructing a URL with query parameters, which character is used to separate the first query parameter from the base URL path?
questions.explanationMd: The query string begins with `?`, such as `/search?q=javascript`. Additional parameters then use `&`.

questions.questionMd: When using ordinary non-arrow inner functions as `fetch()` callbacks inside a class method, how can you correctly fix the `this` binding problem?

options.text: Declare the inner functions using the `var` keyword instead of `const` or `let`, because var-scoped functions automatically inherit the `this` context of their parent scope
Prefix the inner function declarations with the `static` keyword so that `this` inside the function always refers to the class constructor rather than an instance
Call `.bind(this)` on each inner function when passing it to `.then()`, so the enclosing method's `this` is explicitly attached to the callback
Assign the inner functions to class prototype properties before calling `fetch()`, so the JavaScript engine can look up the correct `this` through the prototype chain at call time

questions.explanationMd: Ordinary functions create their own `this` depending on how they are called. Using `.bind(this)` fixes the callback's `this` value to the surrounding class instance.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following best describes a RESTful API?

options.text: A server-side scripting interface where the browser executes remote functions directly by sending the function name and arguments as query parameters
A peer-to-peer data exchange protocol where client and server negotiate a shared schema before any data transfer can begin
A URL-based API where requests are sent as HTTP requests using methods such as GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE to a base URL known as an API endpoint
A binary protocol API where data is encoded in a compact proprietary format and transmitted over persistent TCP connections without any HTTP overhead

questions.explanationMd: A RESTful API exposes resources through URLs and uses standard HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE to interact with those resources.
